awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Decision Support Software for Design Data Center Cooling Systems
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of a software platform that assists in the design of cooling systems for data centers. Data centers serve as the core infrastructure supporting communication networks, online services such as cloud storage and data processing, and high-performance computing. As demand for these facilities rises due to applications such as artificial intelligence, the power required to operate them is skyrocketing, with nearly half of this power being used for cooling. This digital twin software, which provides a virtual online representation of a data center’s cooling system, offers significant advantages to the data center industry, by aiding in more energy efficient operations, longer equipment lifespan, and lower operational costs – all of which are crucial in such a competitive and energy-intensive industry. The technology can also improve the reliability of services that use these data centers, benefiting government and commercial users as well as the general public by ensuring better, more consistent access to digital services and applications.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of a modular simulation framework for analyzing and optimizing the thermal performance, energy efficiency, durability, and cost of electronic cooling networks. The framework integrates several scientific techniques into a unified workflow. A reduced-order thermal model is used to approximate three-dimensional temperature distributions across components, servers, racks, and rooms based on high-fidelity simulation data, enabling rapid assessment of new design configurations. This model is dynamically coupled with a flow solver that computes pressure, temperature, and mass flow rate across interconnected cooling components, including channels with phase-change behavior. The solver supports both single- and two-phase working fluids, making it applicable to traditional air and liquid cooling systems as well as more advanced boiling/evaporation-based techniques. Reliability prediction is incorporated using statistical degradation models and system-level availability metrics. The platform also includes cost estimation routines that compute key financial indicators, such as operational expenses, capital investment requirements, and investment returns, based on modeled performance. This integrated approach enables users to compare cooling strategies not only based on technical performance, but also in terms of long-term cost-effectiveness and system reliability, thus enabling more informed decision-making in the design of data center infrastructure.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

MOSTCOOL NSF I-Corps Project Outcomes Report

Data centers, which house the infrastructure that powers cloud computing, artificial intelligence (AI), and other online services, are increasingly necessary for today’s digital economy. While essential for modern digital services, these facilities require massive amounts of energy and water for cooling. To address this challenge, the ARPA-E COOLERCHIPS-supported MOSTCOOL (Multi-Objective Simulation Tool for Cooling Optimization and Operational Longevity) software was developed to rapidly evaluate and optimize the performance, energy efficiency, reliability, and cost of alternative data center cooling system designs. Its development was done via a multidisciplinary collaboration involving researchers, scientists and engineers at the University of Maryland, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, University of Arkansas, and Trane. Key software features include rapid thermal performance prediction for standard air, single phase liquid, and two-phase cold plate approaches for server cooling, system-level energy and carbon emissions analysis, physics-of-failure reliability modeling, and cost modeling. It is the first software platform to integrate co-simulation and co-optimization of thermal, energy, reliability and cost analyses into a unified framework. By integrating these analyses into a single software platform, MOSTCOOL helps engineers evaluate design trade-offs more efficiently and support the development of energy-efficient data centers.

The team participated in the NSF National I-Corps program during summer 2025 to better understand market needs and position the software for successful commercialization. Direct customer discovery conducted both during and post program identified the key challenges and priorities of prospective end users and decision makers, helping guide the development of the data center design tool. It was determined that co-location data centers, which house the computing infrastructure of multiple organizations, and older data centers seeking to modernize their infrastructure to support state of the art servers are the primary markets with the strongest need and highest potential for early adoption. More specifically, co-location and legacy data centers prioritize flexible and reliable cooling solutions that keep computing equipment operating efficiently, minimize downtime, reduce energy costs, and ensure uninterrupted services.  Identifying systems that provide sufficient cooling with the highest energy efficiency are necessary to allow co-location and legacy data centers to increase computing output without requiring additional input power. Within this market, distinct pain points across stakeholder groups include the slow speed of current cooling design software for design engineers, and challenges balancing operational costs, navigating regulatory compliance, and planning site upgrades for facility managers. Decision makers responsible for selecting cooling solutions require reliable information to confidently compare alternative technologies, evaluate design trade-offs and justify investment decisions. MOSTCOOL can help support these challenges by enabling rapid data center design analysis for development of more resource-efficient data centers.

Validation of the modeling approach has been done to instill greater confidence in the software results, which is a critical requirement for design engineers, data center operators and decision makers. Most recently, the thermal model was used to predict the performance of a membrane-assisted cooling system for 1 MW data center racks, which was then validated against previous experimental data, showing prediction errors below 10%. The results were presented at the ITHERM 2026 conference and received the Prof. Avram Bar-Cohen Best Paper and Best E-Poster Award.

Cooling system optimization software reduces the energy burden of data centers on the community while providing the benefits of greater computing power - eliminating a critical limitation to future data center growth. Beyond advancing data center cooling design, the software also has the potential to support education and workforce development by providing students hands-on experience with advanced engineering design tools like MOSTCOOL that prepare them for careers in engineering and the data center industry. In fact, the software has been introduced as an educational exercise in multiple courses for both graduate and undergraduate students at the University of Maryland.

To support continued software development, a minimum viable product (MVP) was demonstrated to a small group of users participating in the ARPA-E COOLERCHIPS program to gather feedback and identify opportunities for future improvements. At present, software commercialization will be done through a consortium operated under the University of Maryland. This approach allows prospective customers to interact directly with the MVP, provide feedback on its functionality, communicate their needs, and guide ongoing software development through iterative input. A spinout of the technology will be established once development is complete.
